extracted.intended_audience: financial economists, asset-pricing researchers, and advanced graduate students interested in interactions between labor and capital markets
extracted.subtask_description: Developing and implementing a dynamic general-equilibrium asset-pricing model that endogenizes wages and labor contracts to study how labor-market risk sharing interacts with capital markets and to match stylized facts (participation, equity premium, volatility, correlations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for tradability of human capital via labor contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: The non-tradability view of human capital may be misleading because human capital "does trade (in the form of labor contracts)." The model should explicitly account for that fact by deriving wages endogenously as part of a dynamic equilibrium and modeling firms that "write bilateral labor contracts that insure workers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement labor contracts endogenously (not imposed exogenously) so labor markets can share risk; represent firms as parties that can commit to wage payments and thereby act as insurers of worker human-capital risk. Explain how firms' role as insurers affects asset returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain limited asset market participation as an equilibrium outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: The model must be able to generate limited stock/asset market participation not simply as a friction but as an efficient equilibrium outcome: "A Pareto optimal allocation can therefore be achieved even with the 'narrow' asset span ... implying that limited stock market participation is an efficient equilibrium outcome."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show mechanisms (via labor contracts and optimal risk sharing) by which some agents optimally choose not to participate in capital markets, and demonstrate welfare/Pareto properties of that outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproduce a sizable equity risk premium
rubrics_metrics.description: Model should generate a high equity risk premium: "owners of the firm are the ultimate insurers of this human capital risk. Consequently, shareholders must be compensated ... so the risk premium for holding equity is considerably higher than the risk premium for holding pure consumption risk."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parameterize and demonstrate quantitatively that realistic parameter values (risk aversion, risk-free rate, consumption growth and volatility) can produce observed equity premium magnitudes; explain role of inducement for flexible agents to hold equity leading to high returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the disparity between consumption volatility and asset-price volatility
rubrics_metrics.description: Model must account for "the very large disparity in the volatility of consumption and the volatility of asset prices," i.e., consumption volatility is low while asset volatility can be much higher and time-varying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate mechanisms (interaction of labor contracts and equity) producing low consumption volatility but high and state-dependent equity volatility; produce numerical examples/calibration showing the disconnect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate time-varying (state-dependent) correlation between consumption growth and equity returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Model should deliver a "time dependent correlation between consumption growth and asset returns," specifically low/near-zero correlation in bad states and high correlation in good states (matching empirical findings such as Duffee (2005)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show conditional correlations across business-cycle states (e.g., expansions vs recessions) and link these patterns to model quantities like the equity-wealth-to-consumption ratio and heterogeneity in labor productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include heterogeneous agents with flexible vs inelastic (inflexible) labor access
rubrics_metrics.description: The economy must contain heterogeneous agents: inelastic (inflexible) agents who only have access to a single production technology and flexible agents who can choose across technologies. This heterogeneity is central to who provides/receives insurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model production technologies so flexible agents optimally move across industries (b*, f*) while inflexible agents are tied to a fixed (b_i,f_i). Use this to generate differential exposure and insurance roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endogenize wages as part of dynamic equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages must be derived endogenously: "We derive wages endogenously as part of a dynamic equilibrium in a production economy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve for wage processes in equilibrium rather than imposing wage contracts exogenously; show consumption allocations and wage functions consistent with Pareto optimality and market-clearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model labor markets as venues for risk sharing via bilateral contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Labor markets are modeled so that firms "write bilateral labor contracts that insure workers," implying labor contracts are an important risk-sharing mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include binding bilateral employment contracts (subject to practical limitations described in restrictions) and characterize how these contracts provide insurance and interact with firms' financing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include capital markets that allow firms to offload labor-market risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital markets facilitate labor-market risk sharing because "it is there that firms offload the labor market risk they assumed from workers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model firms issuing limited-liability equity and/or debt to raise capital that backs wage commitments; show how capital-market participation by investors provides insurance to wage earners indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match key empirical stylized facts (explicit list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The model should be able to produce/qualitatively match the following stylized facts: (1) limited asset market participation, (2) a seemingly high equity risk premium, (3) the large disparity between consumption volatility and asset-price volatility, and (4) the time-dependent correlation between consumption growth and asset returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When developing/calibrating the model, explicitly evaluate those four target moments and demonstrate quantitative or qualitative agreement with empirical measures (e.g., equity premium levels, conditional correlations, volatility ratios).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify aggregate and idiosyncratic productivity dynamics via a state variable s
rubrics_metrics.description: Human/production risk is modeled with a common state variable s that follows a diffusion; specifically they propose a mean-reverting square-root process: ds = θ( s̄ − s) dt + σ√s dω with 2θ s̄ > σ^2 to ensure positivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use µ(s) and σ(s) smoothness/growth conditions given in the paper; interpret s as business-cycle state, define recession as s < s̄. Ensure assumptions needed for PDEs and numerical solutions hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define production-technology set P and properties of f(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Production technologies P ⊂ [0,1]×[0,K] with properties (0,K)∈P, (1,0)∈P, and additional constraints; assume f(b) (the efficient frontier) is strictly concave, twice continuously differentiable, f'(0)=0, f'(1) = −∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These technical properties ensure KF(s) convexity/differentiability etc.; explicitly state and use these properties to derive Lemmas 1–3 and diffusion behavior of productivity aggregates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume CRRA utility and infinite horizon (or large finite horizon approximation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents are infinitely lived with constant relative risk-aversion (CRRA) utility, u(c) = c^{1−γ}/(1−γ) (log when γ=1), and expected utility integral over infinite horizon; numerical work can use a large finite horizon to approximate the infinite-horizon solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use same γ for all agents to allow representative-agent mapping in complete markets; finite-horizon numerical approach used to obtain uniqueness and avoid bubble/transversality complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impose realistic market/trading restrictions (Restriction 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction 1: (i) Binding contracts cannot be written directly between agents. (ii) Firms may enter into binding contracts with agents subject to: (1) Limited liability may not be violated. (2) Workers and equity holders cannot be required to make payments. (iii) Banks may enter into short term debt contracts with agents and firms, paying an interest rate rs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These restrictions reflect practical market limitations (lack of anonymous matching for individualized contracts, one-sided labor contracts, limited enforceability of agents' payment commitments); incorporate them when demonstrating feasible implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict firms to operate in a single industry (Restriction 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction 2: "Firms are restricted to operate in only one industry. That is, all workers in a firm must have the same b and f."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specialization assumption increases realism and affects implementation of insurance via firms; note model results qualitatively robust if firms operate in finitely many industries but not if a firm operates in every industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a small utility cost of dynamic trading (Restriction 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction 3: Dynamic trading in equity markets imposes a utility cost of ε = 0+ per unit time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This models transaction/effort costs and favors passive strategies; ensures equilibria that do not require active rebalancing dominate ones that do, and justifies passive investment behavior in the implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation via firms issuing limited-liability equity and bank intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: To implement the Pareto-efficient allocation under realistic restrictions, inelastic agents sign binding lifetime employment contracts; firms issue limited-liability equity, deposit capital in banks; flexible agents borrow from banks to buy equity and optimally adjust borrowing so supply of deposits equals loan demand. Dividends and firm capital dynamics are used to make wage payments and keep firm capital nonnegative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the paper's constructive implementation (wages w_I = η A_t K_tot(s_t), w_F = A_t K_F(s_t); dividend rule At max(α K_I(s)+C_t r_s − η K_tot(s),0); dC_t dynamics) to show feasibility. Use this scheme to argue Pareto optimality under given restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive asset-price PDEs and use numerical transforms for solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Asset prices solve a PDE (Proposition 1) with terms involving R(s)=K'_tot(s)/K_tot(s) and T(s)=K''_tot(s)/K_tot(s); transform z = s/(s+1) to bound domain and solve the PDE numerically (Proposition 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the z-transformation to avoid boundary-condition difficulties at s=0 and s=∞, ensure dividend-growth boundedness condition δ(s,t) ≤ c e^{rt} K_tot(s)^γ, and solve PDE (18) numerically; verify convergence and boundary behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce volatility and correlation predictions (Lemma 3 and calibration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model should generate the qualitative volatility patterns: flexible agents' productivity volatility is lower than inflexible agents' for low s, higher for high s (Lemma 3); calibrated model should show equity volatility exploding in bad states and consumption volatility largely unaffected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lemmas to justify the roles of mobility and convexity; calibrate parameters and present state-dependent volatility plots and conditional correlations to compare with empirical facts (e.g., consumption volatility nearly flat, equity volatility highly state-dependent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameterize and calibrate to realistic data to validate quantitative implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Use reasonable parameter values for risk aversion, interest rate, growth, volatility, and production-technology parameters so the model quantitatively matches observed moments: unconditional expected returns, equity risk premium, volatility profiles, and conditional correlations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform numerical calibration (as in Section 5) and compare model-implied moments to empirical counterparts (e.g., equity premium ~8% conditional at certain s, unconditional premium ~4.1%, consumption volatility behavior). Report sensitivity to initial state s0 and discuss economic interpretation.
